params.name: emax
params.let: 6 if b == 2 else (4 if b == 3 else 3)

params.why: the constant in the denominator's exponent must be a positive whole number, otherwise the attempt is thrown away

solution: Use the power law on the bracket in the numerator, multiplying the exponent by 2: $({=b}^{x+{=p}})^{2}={=b}^{2(x+{=p})}={=b}^{2x+{=2 * p}}$.
Use the product law in the numerator, adding the exponents: ${=b}^{2x+{=2 * p}}\times {=b}^{{=q}-x}={=b}^{(2x+{=2 * p})+({=q}-x)}={=b}^{x+{=2 * p + q}}$.

Use the quotient law, subtracting the exponent of the denominator and keeping its brackets: $\dfrac{{=b}^{x+{=2 * p + q}}}{{=b}^{x+{=r}}}={=b}^{(x+{=2 * p + q})-(x+{=r})}={=b}^{x+{=2 * p + q}-x-{=r}}={=b}^{{=k}}$.
The $x$ terms cancel, so evaluate the power: ${=b}^{{=k}}={=b ** k}$.
notes: Modelled on the book's variable-exponent cancellations (ex2-1-14, ex2-1-15, ex2-4-1e), which use the same 'subtract with brackets, then collect' method. The advanced twist is that all three laws are needed in one line: power law on a bracket whose exponent is a sum, product law in the numerator, then the quotient law with a bracketed subtraction, so that the x terms (2x - x - x) cancel and a pure number remains. Parameters: base from 2, 3, 5; the final exponent k is drawn first (2..6 for base 2, 2..4 for base 3, 2..3 for base 5) so the answer never exceeds 125, and r is computed as 2p + q - k and must be at least 1. The statement is true for every real x, and no denominator can be zero. No distractors (numeric answer), so no misconception ids are attached.
